place.zh: 沉鼎观 · 柴房 · 开春

setup.zh: 正月里，家里的回信到了；背面三行是舅舅的字。一冬喂饭桶，开出半垛破烂；雪化的前一夜，柴房里能喂的，只剩小狰嘴里那半截萝卜。
setup.en: In the first month the letter from home came; three lines on the back were your uncle's. A winter of feeding the Rice Tub has brought out half a woodpile of junk; the night before the thaw, the only thing left in the woodshed to feed it is the half radish in the little Zheng's mouth.

recap.zh: 小狰的半截萝卜，饭桶吐出三颗九转筑基丹，你被吸得瘫了一夜：一颗你贴肉揣着，两颗藏进饭桶；开春残株喂出三颗九转聚气丹——阿禾、孙二狗的书案底下，各多了一个油纸包。
recap.en: The little Zheng's half radish, and the Rice Tub gave three nine-turn Foundation pills, and drained you flat for a night: one you carry against your skin, two hidden in the Rice Tub; spring culls fed in gave three nine-turn qi pills — and under A-He's desk and Sun Ergou's, an oilpaper packet each.

en: A winter: half a woodpile of junk.
The half radish in the little Zheng's mouth.
The lid springs open: three, side by side.

story.zh:
信纸背面最底下，还有三行，字大，墨重，一笔一画像拨算盘，是他舅舅的手笔：

腊月里，马家来过一个穿白的，在你家门口站了一夜。你爹搬了条板凳，坐在门槛里头，膝盖上横着那把柴刀，也坐了一夜。天亮，那人走了。

一个穿白的。穿白的，他见过不止一回：开山门那天，河滩上拿银子换孩子的，脸他没敢瞧，嗓子却是那一副；腊八那天，台上那面镜子，马小宝说是「白衣仙长留下的」。可在自家门口一站一夜的，他心里只想得到一个——正月初五那一夜，柴垛底下端铜镜的那一个：脸白得看不出年纪，嗓子又干又深，像一口老井，雪地上不留一个脚印。

他想的却是另一样：他爹那条腿。腊月的夜，门槛里头透风，一条板凳，一把柴刀，一个膝盖，坐到天亮。

他摸了摸袖子里那只辣椒油瓶子——瓶里那颗九纹回春丹，是留给爹的膝盖的。断着肋骨巡那半个月夜，他也没舍得拔一回瓶塞。

这一冬，他隔几夜便喂一回饭桶。它什么都吃，可吃得有高有低：一个月剩下的那一块灵石喂进去，「咯嘣咯嘣」嚼得香，吐出来的东西也像样些；磨穿了的草鞋底喂进去，它打一个嗝，原样吐回来，吐了他一脸；马小宝在饭堂里掉下的半块桂花糕，它倒是吃了，吐出来的是破烂。十回里九回是破烂，柴垛底下塞了半垛，跟那只捆着腿的木头牲口作伴。喂什么都一样的，是开一回，便吸走他一截灵气，第二天讲堂上打瞌睡，褚先生说漏勺又漏了。九道纹的，一颗也没有。

雪化的前一夜，他刚喂过一回，丹田里只剩一层薄底，灵石喂完了，鞋底它不要，柴房里能喂的，只剩小狰嘴里叼着的那半截萝卜。伙房讨来的，一天一根，它吃得极慢，啃一口，看他一眼。

他蹲下来，跟小狰对看了半天。他想起那一夜在药园里，一根萝卜，不值一文钱，它吃饱了，就地睡在一个生人面前。他想要一颗九道纹的筑基丹，想得心里发烫；可丹田里那一层底再吸走，今夜便要瘫在这柴房里，明早讲堂点名，跟班的眼睛就在门口。
story.en:
At the very bottom of the back of the letter were three more lines, big, heavy with ink, each stroke like a flick of an abacus bead — his uncle's hand:

In the twelfth month a man in white came to the Ma house, and stood at your door all night. Your father brought out a bench and sat just inside the threshold with the wood-chopper across his knees, all night too. At dawn the man left.

A man in white. Men in white he had seen more than once: on the day the gate opened, the one on the river flats trading silver for a child — he had not dared look at the face, but the voice was that same voice; on the day of Laba, the mirror on the stage, which Ma Xiaobao said was "left by the Immortal Master in white". But one who would stand a whole night at his own door — he could think of only one: the night of the fifth of the first month, the one under the woodpile holding the bronze mirror: a face so white you could not tell its age, a voice dry and deep like an old well, and not one footprint left in the snow.

But what he thought of was something else: his father's leg. A twelfth-month night, the draught under the threshold, a bench, a wood-chopper, a knee, sitting till dawn.

He felt for the chili-oil bottle in his sleeve — the nine-ring mending pill in it was kept for his father's knee. Through that half-month of night rounds on a broken rib he had not once let himself pull the stopper.

All that winter he fed the Rice Tub every few nights. It ate anything, but not everything alike: the one spirit stone left from each month went in with a crunch, *crack, crack*, chewed with relish, and what came out was a little more like something; a sandal sole worn through went in, and it gave a burp and spat it straight back out into his face; half an osmanthus cake Ma Xiaobao had dropped in the refectory, it did eat, and what came out was junk. Nine times in ten it was junk; it filled half the woodpile, keeping company with the wooden beast with its legs tied. What every feeding had in common: each time it opened, it drew off a share of his qi, and next day he dozed in the lecture hall, and Master Chu said the skimmer had leaked again. Of nine-ring pills, not one.

The night before the snow melted, he had just fed it once already; only a thin floor of qi was left in his dantian. The stones were fed, the sandal sole it wouldn't have, and the only thing left in the woodshed to feed it was the half radish in the little Zheng's mouth. Begged from the kitchen, one a day; it ate very slowly, a bite, then a look at him.

He squatted down, and he and the little Zheng looked at each other a long while. He remembered that night in the herb garden: a radish, not worth one copper, and it had eaten its fill and fallen asleep right there in front of a stranger. He wanted a nine-ring Foundation pill so badly it burned; but let that last floor of qi be drawn off, and tonight he would be lying flat in this woodshed, and tomorrow there was roll call in the lecture hall, with the hangers-on's eyes at the door.

label.en: The half radish — feed it in

exits.means: puts the culls and the two ginseng roots into the furnace and makes pills

story.zh:
他伸手，把那半截萝卜从小狰嘴里拔了出来。小狰两只前爪还保持着抱萝卜的样子，愣在那里，瞧着空了的爪子，又瞧着他。他把萝卜塞进饭桶，两只手按上铜肚子：「……就这一回。明天赔你两根。」

饭桶这一回吸得极狠，不像往常一口一口地吸，倒像有人揪住他丹田里那一层底，连根往外拔。他眼前一黑，手却没松；再一黑，人便往前一栽，额头磕在盖子上，什么也不知道了。

醒过来的时候，天已经亮了。他趴在柴房的泥地上，半边脸贴着地，浑身软得像一根泡过水的面条，手指头都抬不起来；小狰蹲在他鼻子跟前，背对着他，尾巴一甩一甩，还在生气。饭桶的盖子开着，盖上那只小兽还在打盹，睡得极沉，像是夜里吃了什么，也没看清。肚里并排躺着三颗丹。他攒了半天力气，拈起一颗对着窗缝里的光一照，登时呆了。那丹的模样，跟玉盒子里那颗筑基丹一般无二，只不过那颗褐里透红，一道纹，还带着几点黑斑；这三颗却透亮得像三滴凝住的露水，一丝杂色也无，丹身上九道纹，金灿灿的。

他把袖子里那只辣椒油瓶子摸出来，跟这三颗并排一摆，冲小狰小声道：「听好了：炼一转，多一道纹。玉盒里那颗，一道，带毒；这三颗，九道。瓶里这颗也是九道，可它是回春丹，治伤的，留给爹的膝盖——你别给我叼混了。」小狰打了个喷嚏，把脑袋扭到一边去了。

当下打定了主意：一颗，是自己的；另外两颗，用油纸裹了三层，塞回饭桶肚里，跟那只玉盒子作伴。

第二天夜里，他又从伙房讨了一根萝卜，喂了进去，搓着手等。盖子底下半天没有动静。过了一会儿，「噗」的一声，炉口喷出一股黑烟，不偏不倚，正喷在他脸上，喷完了，盖子「咔哒」一合，再按，按不开了。小满顶着一张黑脸，小狰在一旁看着他，打了一个响鼻。他道：「……这桶，是不是在生气？」一连三夜，那盖子都没给他开。

好容易熬到开了春，雪一化，药园开了园，周衡那一篮残株便送到了。这是小满巡夜的工钱，虫咬的，长歪的，灵气散了一半的，满满一篮，周衡递给他的时候，照例在账簿上记一笔：「残株一篮。扔。」

那一篮残株，他嚼一株，喂它一株，手气竟像是转了：半个月里，破烂堆里开出三颗聚气丹来，也是九道纹；外门份例里每月一颗的，是一道纹的。第三颗，他当夜自己吃了，丹田里「哗」的一声，像是有人往那口水缸里倒了一桶水，前些天给饭桶吸走的，一并补了回来。这一年，十回里总有一回开出一颗九转聚气丹来，一个月一颗上下。

过了两日，讲堂上阿禾的书案底下多了一个油纸包，纸包里一颗聚气丹，一张纸条：**一个鸡蛋的利息。**孙二狗的书案底下也多了一个，纸条上写的是：**牛棚里那半张饼的利息。**

天亮的时候，孙二狗从练气零层，冲到了一层。

他站在大通铺门口，把一只手摊在太阳底下，瞧着掌心里那一缕细细的黄气，瞧得眼泪鼻涕一齐流了下来。

这一哭，哭坏了事。一个零层的杂灵根，一夜引了气，不到晌午便传遍了外门；传到马小宝耳朵里，只剩一句：沈小满手里有丹，好丹。
story.en:
He reached out and pulled the half radish out of the little Zheng's mouth. The little Zheng's front paws stayed just as they were, hugging a radish that wasn't there; it sat frozen, looking at its empty paws, then at him. He pushed the radish into the Rice Tub and pressed both hands on the bronze belly: "…Just this once. Two for you tomorrow."

This time the Rice Tub drew terribly hard — not mouthful by mouthful as usual, but as if someone had seized that last floor in his dantian and was pulling it out by the roots. His sight went black, and his hands did not let go; it went black again, and he pitched forward, his forehead struck the lid, and he knew nothing more.

When he came to, it was already light. He lay face down on the earth floor of the woodshed, half his face in the dirt, limp all over as a noodle left in water, unable to lift a finger; the little Zheng sat in front of his nose with its back to him, tail flicking, still sulking. The Rice Tub's lid was open, and the little beast on it was still dozing, sleeping deep, as if it had eaten something in the night without looking. In its belly lay three pills side by side. He gathered his strength a long while, picked one up, held it to the light from the crack in the window, and froze. It looked exactly like the Foundation pill in the jade box — except that one was brown shot with red, with one ring and a few dark flecks, and these three were as clear as three drops of frozen dew, not a speck of other colour in them, with nine rings each, bright gold.

He took the chili-oil bottle out of his sleeve, set it beside the three, and said to the little Zheng under his breath: "Listen: every turn in the refining adds one ring. The one in the jade box has one ring, and poison; these three have nine. The one in the bottle has nine too, but it's a mending pill, for wounds — it's for Father's knee. Don't you go mixing them up." The little Zheng sneezed and turned its head away.

He made up his mind on the spot: one was his; the other two, wrapped in three layers of oilpaper, went back into the Rice Tub's belly to keep the jade box company.

The next night he begged another radish from the kitchen, fed it in, and waited, rubbing his hands. Nothing stirred under the lid for a long while. Then — *pff* — a puff of black smoke shot out of the mouth, straight into his face; the lid clicked shut, and when he pressed it, it wouldn't open. Xiaoman sat with a black face, and the little Zheng looked at him and snorted. He said: "…Is this tub sulking?" For three nights running, the lid would not open for him.

At last spring came; the snow melted, the herb garden opened, and Zhou Heng's basket of culls arrived. It was Xiaoman's pay for the night watch — worm-eaten, crooked, half their spirit gone, a full basket — and as Zhou Heng handed it over he made his usual entry in the ledger: "Culls, one basket. Thrown out."

That basket of culls — he chewed one, fed it one, and his luck seemed to turn: in half a month, out of the junk came three qi pills, nine rings too; the ones in the outer court's monthly allowance had one ring. The third he ate himself that night, and his dantian went *whoosh*, as if someone had tipped a bucket of water into the great jar — what the Rice Tub had drawn off those last days came back all at once. That year, about one time in ten it brought out a nine-turn qi pill — roughly one a month.

Two days later there was an oilpaper packet under A-He's desk in the lecture hall, a qi pill in it and a slip of paper: **Interest on one egg.** There was one under Sun Ergou's desk too, and its slip said: **Interest on half a flatbread in the cowshed.**

At daybreak, Sun Ergou broke from Qi Condensation layer zero to layer one.

He stood at the dormitory door with one hand held open in the sun, looking at the thin yellow wisp of qi in his palm, until tears and snot ran down together.

That crying spoiled everything. A mixed-root boy at layer zero drawing in qi in a single night — before noon the whole outer court knew it; by the time it reached Ma Xiaobao's ears, only one sentence was left: Shen Xiaoman has pills, good ones.
